Quosvis authores absurdis commentis suis percacant & stercorant, one saith, they beray and daub a company of books and good Authors, with their absurd Comments, correctorum sterquilinia [the dunghills of proofreaders] Lib. 2 in Ausonium, cap. 19 & 32.Scaliger calls them, and show their wit in censuring others, a company of foolish note-makers, humble-bees, dors or beetles, inter stercora ut plurimum versantur, they rake over all those rubbish and dunghills, and prefer a manuscript many times before the Gospel itself, Edit. 7 volum. a Jano Grutero.thesaurum criticum [a collection of criticism], before any treasure, and with their deleatur d, alii legunt sic, meus codex sic habet [‘d’ should be deleted, others read in this way, my manuscript has this], with their postremae editiones [latest editions], annotations, castigations, &c., make books dear, themselves ridiculous, and do nobody good, yet if any man dare oppose or contradict, they are mad, up in arms on a sudden, how many sheets are written in defence, how bitter invectives, what apologies? Aristophanis Ranis.Epiphilledes hae sunt ut merae nugae [These are mere gleanings and pure trifles]. But I dare say no more of, for, with, or against them, because I am liable to their lash, as well as others. Of these and the rest of our Artists and Philosophers, I will generally conclude they are a kind of madmen, as Lib. de beneficiis.Seneca esteems of them, to make doubts & scruples, how to read them truly, to mend old authors, but will not mend their own lives, or teach us ingenia sanare, memoriam officiorum ingerere, ac fidem in rebus humanis retinere [to correct character, to impress the memory of services upon their minds, and maintain faith in human affairs], to keep our wits in order, or rectify our manners. Numquid tibi demens videtur, si istis operam impenderit? [Wouldn’t he seem crazy to you if he expended effort on such things?] Is not he mad that draws lines with Archimedes, while his house is ransacked, and his city besieged, when the whole world is in combustion, or we whilst our souls are in danger (mors sequitur, vita fugit [death chases, life flees]) to spend our time in toys, idle questions, and things of no worth?

That Delirus & amens dicatur merito [He would justly be said to be crazy and out of his mind]. Hor. Seneca.Lovers are mad, I think no man will deny, Amare simul & sapere, ipsi Jovi non datur [even Jupiter isn’t permitted to love and be wise at the same time], Jupiter himself cannot intend both at once,

l.hi: Non bene conveniunt, nec in una sede morantur

lg.l: Majestis & amor.
[They do not combine well, nor do they dwell together:
Majesty and love.]

div.p: Tully when he was invited to a second marriage, replied, he could not simul amare & sapere, be wise and love both together. Plutarch. Amatorio. Est amor insanus [Love is insane].Est orcus ille, vis est immedicabilis, est rabies insana, Love is madness, a hell, an incurable disease; impotentem & insanam libidinem Epist. 39.Seneca calls it, an impotent and raging lust. I shall dilate this subject apart; in the meantime let Lovers sigh out the rest.

Sylvae nuptialis. lib. 1 num. 11.Nevisanus the Lawyer holds it for an axiom, most women are fools, Aristotle.consilium faeminis invalidum [the judgement of women is weak]; Seneca men, be they young or old; who doubts it, youth is mad as Laelius in Tully, stulti adolescentuli [foolish young men], old age little better, deliri senes, &c. [crazy old men, etc.] Theophrastus in the 107th year of his age, Dolere se dixit quod tum vita egrederetur [He said he was pained because then life was departing].said he then began to be wise, tum sapere caepit, and therefore lamented his departure. If wisdom come so late, where shall we find a wise man? Our old ones dote at threescore and ten. I would cite more proofs, and a better Author, but for the present, let one fool point at another. Lib. 4 num. 11.Nevisanus hath as hard an opinion of They get their wisdom by eating Piecrust some.rich men, wealth and wisdom cannot dwell together, stultitiam patiuntur opes [wealth supports foolishness], Χρήματα τοῖς θνητοῖς γίγνεται ἀφροσύνη. Opes quidem mortalibus sunt amentia [Wealth becomes madness for men]. Theognis.and they do commonly Fortuna nimium quem fovet, stultum facit [Fortune makes a fool of the man whom she favours too much].infatuare cor hominis [infatuate the heart of man], besot men; and as we see it, fools have fortune: Job. 28.Sapientia non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium [wisdom is not found in the land of those living sweetly]. For beside a natural contempt of learning, which accompanies such kind of men, innate idleness (for they will take no pains), and which Mag. moral. lib. 2 & lib. 1 metaph.Aristotle observes, ubi mens plurima, ibi minima fortuna, ubi plurima fortuna, ibi mens perexigua [where there’s much understanding, there is very little fortune, where there is much fortune, there’s very little understanding], great wealth and little wit go commonly together: they have as much brains some of them in their heads as in their heels; besides this inbred neglect of liberal sciences, and all Arts, which should excolere mentem, polish the mind, they have most part some gullish humour or other, by which they are led; one
is an Epicure, an Atheist, a second a gamester, a third a whoremaster (fit subjects all for a Satirist to work upon),

lg.l: ——— Hor. ser. 1 sat. 4.Hic nuptarum insanit amoribus, hic puerorum,
[… one is crazy for married women, another for boys,]

div.p: Insana gula, insanae substructiones, insanum venandi studium, discordia demens [Insane gluttony, insane basements, insane zeal for hunting, demented discord]. Virg. Aen.one is mad of hawking, hunting, cocking; another of carousing, horse-riding, spending; a fourth of building, fighting, &c.

l.hi: Insanit veteres statuas Damasippus emendo,

lg.l: [Damasippus is crazy about buying old statues,]

div.p: Damasippus hath a humour of his own, to be talked of: Heliodorus insanus Carthaginensis ad extremum orbis sarcophago testamento me hic jussi condier, & ut viderem an quis insanior ad me visendum usque ad haec loca penetraret [The madman Heliodorus of Carthage ordered that I be built here as a memorial tomb at the end of the world, to see whether any madder man would make his way as far as this place in order to see me]. Ortelius in Gad.Heliodorus the Carthaginian another. In a word, as Scaliger concludes of them all, they are statuae erectae stultitiae, the very statues or pillars of folly. Choose out of all stories him that hath been most admired, you shall still find, multa ad laudem, multa ad vituperationem magnifica [many great things to praise, many to blame], as If it be his work, which Gasper Varrerius suspects.Berosus of Semiramis; omnes mortales militia, triumphis, divitiis, &c., tum & luxu, caede, caeterisque vitiis antecessit [she exceeded all mortals in wars, triumphs, riches, etc., but also in debauchery, murder, and other vices], as she had some good, so had she many bad parts.

Alexander, a worthy man, but furious in his anger, overtaken in drink: Caesar and Scipio valiant and wise, but vainglorious, ambitious: Vespasian a worthy Prince, but covetous: Livy, Ingentes virtutes ingentia vitia [Prodigious virtues, prodigious vices].Hannibal, as he had mighty virtues, so had he many vices; unam virtutem mille vitia comitantur [a thousand vices accompany one virtue], as Machiavel of Cosmus Medices, he had two distinct persons in him. I will determine of them all, they are like these double or turning pictures; stand before which, you see a fair maid, on the one side an ape, on the other an owl; look upon them at the first sight all is well, but further examine, you shall find them wise on the one side, and fools on the other; in some few things praiseworthy, in the rest incomparably faulty. I will say nothing of their diseases, emulations, discontents, wants, and such miseries; let poverty plead the rest in Aristophanes’ Plutus.
Covetous men amongst others, are most mad, Hor. ser. 2 sat. 3.they have all the Symptoms of melancholy, fear, sadness, suspicion, &c., as shall be proved in his proper place,

lg.l: Danda est Hellebori multo pars maxima avaris.
[The covetous man must be given by far the largest dose of Hellebore.]

div.p: And yet methinks prodigals are much madder than they, be of what condition they will, that bear a public, or private purse; as a Cronica Slavonica ad annum 1257 de cujus pecunia jam incredibilia dixerunt [The Slavonic Chronicles for the year 1257 related now incredible things about his wealth].Dutch writer censured Richard the rich Duke of Cornwall, suing to be Emperor, for his profuse spending, qui effudit pecuniam ante pedes principium Electorum sicut aquam, that scattered money [at the feet of the prince-electors] like water; I do censure them, Stulta Anglia (saith he) quae tot denariis sponte est privata, stulti principes Alemaniae, qui nobile jus suum pro pecunia vendiderunt [foolish England, that was voluntarily deprived of so much money, foolish German princes, who sold their noble right {as electors} for cash]; spendthrifts, bribers, and bribe-takers are fools, and so are A fool and his money are soon parted.all they that cannot keep, disburse, or spend their moneys well.

I might say the like of angry, peevish, envious, Hor. Quisquis ambitione mala aut argenti pallet amore, quisquis luxuria, tristique superstitione [Whoever turns pale with evil ambition or love of money, whoever with extravagance, with dismal superstition].ambitious; Per.Anticyras melior sorbere meracas [better to swallow {the hellebore of} the Anticyras undiluted]; Epicures, Atheists, Schismatics, Heretics; hi omnes habent imaginationem laesam [all these people have damaged imagination] (saith Orat. de Imag. Ambitiosus & audax naviget Anticyras [Let the ambitious and foolhardy man sail to the Anticyras].Nymannus), and their madness shall be evident, 2 Tim. 3. 9. Gaspar Ens Moros.Fabatus an Italian, holds seafaring men all mad; the ship is mad, for it never stands still: the mariners are mad, to expose themselves to such imminent dangers: the waters are raging mad, in perpetual motion: the winds are as mad as the rest, they know not whence they come, whither they would go: and those men are maddest of all that go to sea; for one fool at home, they find forty abroad. He was a madman that said it, and thou peradventure as mad to read it. Cap. de alien. mentis.Felix Platerus is of opinion all Alchemists are mad, out of their wits; Dipnosophist. lib. 8.Athenaeus saith as much of Fiddlers, & musarum luscinias [and nightingales of the Muses], Tibicines mente capti [Pipers out of their mind]. Erasm. Chil. 4 cent. 7.Musicians, omnes tibicines insaniunt, ubi semel efflant, avolat illico mens [all pipers are crazy: as soon as they start blowing, their mind instantly flies away], in comes music at one ear, out goes wit at another. Proud and vainglorious persons are certainly mad; and so are Prov. 30. Insana libido. Hic rogo non furor est, non est haec mentula demens [Raging lust: ‘Isn’t this madness?’ I ask. ‘Isn’t this a demented penis?’]. Mart. ep. 76 lib. 3.lascivious; I can feel their pulses beat hither, horn-mad some of them, to let others lie with their wives, and wink at it.

To insist Mille puellarum & puerorum mille furores [Thousands of passions for boys and girls].in all particulars, were an Herculean task, to Uter est insanior horum [Which of these two is more insane?]. Hor. Ovid. Virg. Plin.reckon up Plin. lib. 36.insanas substructiones, insanos labores, insanum luxum [mad basements, mad works, mad excess], mad labours, mad books, endeavours, carriages, gross ignorance, ridiculous actions, absurd gestures; insanam gulam, insaniam villarum, insana jurgia [mad gluttony, the madness of villas, mad quarrels], as Tully terms them, madness of villages, stupend structures; as those Egyptian Pyramids, Labyrinths and Sphinxes, which a company of crowned asses, ad ostentationem opum [for the display of riches], vainly built, when neither the Architect nor King that made them, or to what use and purpose, are yet known: to insist in their hypocrisy, inconstancy, blindness, rashness, dementem temeritatem [demented foolhardiness], fraud, cozenage, malice, anger, impudence, ingratitude, ambition, gross superstition, Tacitus 3 Annal.tempora infecta & adulatione sordida [the times stained and fouled by adulation], as in Tiberius’ times, such base flattery, stupend, parasitical fawning and colloguing, &c., brawls, conflicts, desires, contentions, it would ask an expert Vesalius to anatomize every member. Shall I say? Jupiter himself, Apollo, Mars, &c., doted; and monster-conquering Hercules that subdued the world, & helped others, could not relieve himself in this, but mad he was at last. And where shall a man walk, converse with whom, in what Province, City, and not meet with Signior Deliro, or Hercules Furens, Maenades, and Corybantes? Their speeches say no less. Ovid. 7 met. E fungis nati homines ut olim Corinthi primaevi illius loci accolae, quia stolidi & fatui fungis nati dicebantur, idem & alibi dicas [They are men begotten of mushrooms, as once upon a time those who dwelled near ancient Corinth were said to be, because of their stolidity and foolishness; you could say the same of other places too].E fungis nati homines [Men born of mushrooms], or else they fetched their pedigree from those that were struck by Samson with the jawbone of an ass. Or from Deucalion and Pyrrha’s stones, for durum genus sumus, Famian. Strada de bajulis, de marmore semisculptis [Famiano Strada on porters, half-carved from marble].marmorei sumus [we’re a hard race, we’re made of marble] we are stony-hearted, and savour too much of the stock, as if they had all heard that enchanted horn of Astolpho that English Duke in Ariosto, which never sounded but all his auditors were mad, & for fear ready to make away themselves; Arrianus periplo maris Euxini portus ejus meminit [Arrian remembers this port in his Periplus of the Euxine Sea], & Gillius lib. 3. de Bosphor. Thracio. & laurus insana quae allata in convivium convivas omnes insania affecit [And the insane laurel, brought to a feast, which infected all the guests with madness]. Guliel. Stuckius comment, &c.or landed in the mad haven in the Euxine sea of Daphnis insana [Daphne the Insane], which had a secret quality to dementate; they are a company of giddy-heads, afternoon men, it is Midsummer moon still, and the Dog days last all the year long, they are all mad. Whom shall I then except? Ulricus Huttenus Lepidum poema sic inscriptum [A charming poem with this title].nemo, nam, nemo omnibus horis sapit, Nemo nascitur sine vitiis, Crimine Nemo caret, Nemo sorte sua vivit contentus, Nemo in amore sapit, Nemo bonus, Nemo sapiens, Nemo, est ex omni parti beatus, &c. [Nobody, for Nobody is wise all
the time, Nobody is born without faults, Nobody is free from reproach, Nobody lives content with his own lot, Nobody is wise in love, Nobody is good, Nobody is wise, Nobody is fortunate in every respect, etc.], and therefore Nicholas Nemo, or Monsieur Nobody shall go free, Quid valeat nemo, Nemo referre potest? [what’s Nobody capable of? Nobody can answer.] But whom shall I except in the second place? Such as are silent, vir sapit qui pauca loquitur [he is wise who says little]; no better way to avoid folly and madness, than by taciturnity. Whom in a third? All Senators, Magistrates; for all fortunate men are wise, and conquerors valiant, and so are all great men, non est bonum ludere cum diis [it’s not good to mock the gods], they are wise by authority, good by their office and place, his licet impune pessimos esse [they are allowed to be wicked with impunity] (some say), we must not speak of them, neither is it fit; per me sint omnia protinus alba [I will whitewash everything forthwith], I will not think amiss of them. Whom next? Stoics? Sapiens Stoicus [The Stoic Sage], and he alone is subject to no perturbations, as Plutarch scoffs at him, he is not vexed with torments, or burnt with fire, foiled by his adversary, sold of his enemy: though he be wrinkled, sand-blind, toothless and deformed; yet he is most beautiful, and like a god, a king in conceit, though not worth a groat. He never dotes, never mad, never sad, drunk, because virtue cannot be taken away, as Lipsius phys. Stoic. lib. 3 dissi. 18.Zeno holds, by reason of strong apprehension, but he was mad to say so. Tarraeus Hebius epig. 102 lib. 8.Anticyrae caelo huic est opus aut dolabra [He needs the air of Anticyra or a pickaxe], he had need to be bored, and so had all his fellows, as wise as they would seem to be. Chrysippus himself liberally grants them to be fools as well as others, at certain times, upon some occasions, amitti virtutem ait per ebrietatem, aut atribilarium morbum, it may be lost by drunkenness or melancholy, he may be sometimes crazed as well as the rest: Hor.ad summum sapiens nisi quum pituita molesta [supremely wise, except when troubled by phlegm]. I should here except some Cynics, Menippus, Diogenes, that Theban Crates; or to descend to these times, that omniscious, only wise fraternity of the Rosy Cross, those great Theologues, Politicians, Philosophers, Physicians, Philologers, Artists, &c., of whom St. Bridget, Abbas Joachimus, Liechtenbergius, and such divine spirits have prophesied, & made promise to the world, if at least there be any such (Hen. An sint, quales sint, unde nomen illud asciverint [Whether they exist, what kind of men they are, whence they have received their name].Neuhusius makes a doubt of it, Turri Babel.Valentinus Andreas and others), or an Elias artifex their Theophrastian master; whom though Libavius & many deride and carp at, yet some will have to be the renewer of all arts & sciences, reformer of the world, & now living, for so Johannes Montanus Strigoniensis that great Patron of Paracelsus contends, and certainly avers Author notarum in epist. Rog. Bacon. edit. Hamburg. 1608.a most divine man, & the quintessence of wisdom wheresoever he is; for he, his fraternity, friends, &c., are all betrothed to wisdom, if
we may believe their disciples and followers. I must needs except Solus hic est sapiens alii volitant velut umbrae [This one alone is wise, the others flutter about like shadows].Lipsius & the Pope, and expunge their name out of the catalogue of fools. For besides that parasitical testimony of Dousa,

l.hi: A Sole exoriente Maeotidas usque paludes,
Nemo est qui Justo se aequiparare queat,

lg.l: [From the rising sun to the swamps of Maeotis,
There’s nobody who can be compared to Justus,]

div.p: Lipsius saith of himself, that he was In epist. ad Balthas. Moretum.humani generis quidem paedagogus voce & stylo [with voice and pen, truly the schoolmaster of mankind], a grand Signior, a Master, a Tutor of us all, and for 13 years he brags, how he sowed wisdom in the Low Countries, as Ammonius the philosopher sometimes did in Alexandria, Rejectiunculae ad Batavum.cum humanitate literas & sapientiam cum prudentia: antistes sapientiae [literature with humanity and wisdom with prudence: the high priest of wisdom], he shall be Sapientium Octavus [the Eighth Sage]. The Pope is more than a man, as Felinus cum reliquis [Felinus with the rest].his parasites often make him, a demigod, and besides his holiness cannot err, in Cathedra [on the throne] belike: and yet some of them have been Magicians, Heretics, Atheists, children, and as Platina saith of John 22, Et si vir literatus, multa stoliditatem & laevitatem prae se ferentia egit, stolidi & socordis vir ingenii [although he was a learned man, he did much that showed stupidity and fickleness, a man of dull and sluggish wit], a scholar sufficient, yet many things he did foolishly, lightly. I can say no more then in particular, but in general terms to the rest, they are all mad, their wits are evaporated, and as Ariosto feigns lib. 34, kept in jars above the Moon.

l.hi: Some lose their wits with love, some with ambition,

lg.l: Some following Magnum virum sequi est sapere [To follow a great man is to be wise], some think; others desipere [{think} it is to be silly].Lords and men of high condition.

l.hi: Some in fair jewels rich and costly set,

lg.l: Others in Catullus.Poetry their wits forget.

l.hi: Another thinks to be an Alchemist,

lg.l: Till all be spent, and that his number’s missed.

div.p: Convict fools they are, madmen upon record; and I am afraid past cure many of them, Plautus Menec.crepunt inguina [their guts are rumbling], the Symptoms are manifest, they are all of Gotham parish:

l.hi: Quum furor haud dubius, quum sit manifesta phrenesis,

lg.l: [When it’s undoubtedly madness, when it’s palpable frenzy,]

div.p: what remains then Or to send for a cook to the Anticyrae to make Hellebore pottage, settle-brain pottage.but to send for Lorarios, those Officers to carry them all together for company to Bedlam, and set Rabelais to be their physician.

If any man shall ask in the meantime, who I am that so boldly censure others, tu nullane habes vitia? [do you have no vices?] Have I no faults? Aliquantulum tamen inde me solabor, quod una cum multis & sapientibus & celeberrimis viris ipse insipiens sim, quod de se Menippus Luciani in Necyomantia [Hence I take a little consolation in that I am one fool among many men both wise and famous, as Lucian’s Menippus says of himself in The Descent into Hades].Yes more than thou hast, whatsoever thou art. Nos numerus sumus [We’re mere ciphers], I confess it again, I am as foolish, as mad as anyone.

l.hi: Insanus vobis videor, non deprecor ipse,

lg.l: Quo minus insanus, ———
[I seem mad to you; I’m not so mad
That I object to that …]

div.p: I do not deny it, demens de populo dematur [let the madman be removed from the public]. My comfort is, I have more fellows, and those of excellent note. And though I be not so right, or so discreet as I should be, yet not so mad, so bad neither as thou perhaps takest me to be.

To conclude, this being granted, that all the world is melancholy, or mad, dotes, and every member of it, I have ended my task, and sufficiently illustrated that which I took upon me to demonstrate at first. At this present I have no more to say; His sanam mentem Democritus [Democritus {wishes} them a sound mind], I can but wish myself, & them a good Physician, and all of us a better mind.

And although for the above-named reasons, I had a just cause to undertake this subject, to point at these particular species of dotage, that so men might acknowledge their imperfections, and seek to reform what is amiss; yet I have a more serious intent at this time; and to omit all impertinent digressions, to say no more of such as are improperly melancholy, or metaphorically mad, lightly mad, or in disposition, as stupid, angry, drunken, silly, sottish, sullen, proud, vainglorious, ridiculous, beastly, peevish, obstinate, impudent, extravagant, dry, doting, dull, desperate, hare-brain, &c., mad, frantic, foolish, heteroclites, which no new That I mean of Andr. Vale. Apolog. manip. lib. 1 & 26 Apol.Hospital can hold, no physic help: my purpose and endeavour is, in the following discourse to anatomize this humour of melancholy, through all his parts and species, as it is an habit, or an ordinary disease, and that philosophically, medicinally, to show the causes, symptoms, and several cures of it, that it may be the better avoided. Moved thereunto for the generality of it, and to do good, it being a disease so frequent, as Mercurialis observes, in these our days; so often happening, saith Cap. 15 de Mel.Laurentius, in our miserable times, as few there are that feel not the smart of it. Of the same mind is Aelian Montaltus, De anima. Nostro hoc saeculo morbus frequentissimus [The most frequent disease of this our age].Melanchthon, and others; Consult. 98. Adeo nostris temporibus frequenter ingruit ut nullus fere ab ejus labe immunis reperiatur & omnium fere morborum occasio existat [In our times, indeed, it frequently strikes, so that scarcely anyone is found free from its stain and it becomes the occasion for almost all diseases].
Julius Caesar Claudinus calls it the fountain of all other diseases, and so common in this crazed age of ours, that scarce one of a thousand is free from it: and that Splenetic Hypochondriacal wind especially, which proceeds from the spleen and short ribs. Being then as it is, a disease so grievous, so common, I know not wherein to do a more general service, and spend my time better, than to prescribe means how to prevent and cure so universal a malady, an Epidemical disease, that so often, so much crucifies the body and mind.

If have overshot myself in this which hath been hitherto said, or that it is, which I am sure some will object, too fantastical, too light and comical for a Divine, too satirical for one of my profession, I will presume to answer with Mor. Encom. Si quis calumnietur levius esse quam decet Theologum, aut mordacius quam deceat Christianum [If anyone should slander me as being more light-hearted than becomes a theologian, or more biting than would become a Christian].Erasmus, in like case, ’tis not I, but Democritus, Democritus dixit [Democritus said it]: you must consider what it is to speak in one’s own or another’s person, an assumed habit and name; a difference betwixt him that affects or acts a Prince’s, a Philosopher’s, a Magistrate’s, a Fool’s part, and him that is so indeed; and what liberty those old Satirists have had, it is a Cento collected from others, not I, but they that say it.

l.hi: Dixero si quid forte jocosius, hoc mihi juris

lg.l: Cum venia dabis ———
[If I’ve accidentally said anything too jokingly,
You’ll kindly grant me this right …]

div.p: Take heed you mistake me not. If I do a little forget myself, I hope you will pardon it. And to say truth, why should any man be offended, or take exceptions at it?

lg.l: ——— Licuit, semperque licebit,
Parcere personis, dicere de vitiis.
It lawful was of old, and still will be,
To speak of vice, but let the name go free:

div.p:
I hate their vices, not their persons. If any be displeased, or take aught unto himself, let him not expostulate or cavil with him that said it (so did Epist. ad Dorpium de Moria.Erasmus excuse himself to Dorpius, si parva licet componere magnis [if we may compare small things with great], and so do I); but let him be angry with himself, that so betrayed and opened his own faults in applying it to himself: Si quis se laesum clamabit, aut conscientiam prodit suam, aut certe metum [If anyone is going to cry about being hurt, he betrays either his own conscience, or at least his fear].If he be guilty and deserve it, let him amend whoever he is, and not be angry. He that
hateth correction is a fool, Prov. 12. 1. If he be not guilty, it concerns him not; it is not my freeness of speech, but a guilty conscience, a galled back of his own that makes him winch.

l.hi: Suspitione si quis errabit sua,
Et rapiet ad se, quod erit commune omnium,

lg.l: Stulte nudabit animi conscientiam.
[If anyone errs out of his own suspicion,
And applies to himself what is meant for everyone,
He will foolishly lay bare his bad conscience.]

div.p: I deny not this which I have said savours a little of Democritus; Hor.Quamvis ridentem dicere verum quid vetat; one may speak in jest, and yet speak truth. It is somewhat tart, I grant it; acriora orexim excitant embammata, as he said, sharp sauces increase appetite,

lg.l: Martial. lib. 7. 25.Nec cibus ipse juvat morsu fraudatus aceti.
[Food doesn’t taste good on its own, when the tang of vinegar is removed.]

div.p: Object then and cavil what thou wilt, I ward all with Ut lubet feriat, abstergam hos ictus Democriti Pharmaco [Let him strike as he wishes, I shall wipe the wound clean with the medicine of Democritus].Democritus’ buckler, his medicine shall salve it; strike where thou wilt, and when: Democritus dixit [Democritus said it], Democritus will answer it. It was written by an idle fellow, at idle times, about our Saturnalian or Dionysian feasts, when as he said, nullum libertati periculum est [there’s no danger in liberty], servants in old Rome had liberty to say and do what them list. When our countrymen sacrificed to their goddess Rusticorum dea praesse vacantibus & otiosis putabatur, cui post labores agricola sacrificabat [The goddess of the country people was thought to preside over the unemployed and idle; the farmer sacrificed to her after his work]. Plin. lib. 3 cap. 12. Ovid. lib. 6 Fast. Jam quoque cum fiunt antiquae sacra Vacunae, ante Vacunales stantque sedentque focos [Even now, when sacrifices are made to the ancient goddess Vacuna, they stand and sit before her hearths]. Rosinus.Vacuna, and sat tippling by their Vacunal fires, I writ this, and published this. Οὔτις ἔλεγεν [Nobody was speaking], it is neminis nihil [nothing by nobody]. The time, place, persons, and all circumstances apologize for me, and why may I not then be idle with others? Speak my mind freely? If you deny me this liberty, upon these presumptions I will take it: I say again, I will take it.

l.hi: Si quis est qui dictum in se inclementius

lg.l: Existimavit esse, sic existimet.
[If anyone thinks what’s been said about him
To be too severe, let him think that.]

div.p: If any man take exceptions, let him turn the buckle of his girdle, I care not. I owe thee nothing (Reader), I look for no favour at thy hands, I am independent, I fear not.
No, I recant, I will not, I care, I fear, I confess my fault, acknowledge a great offence,

lg.l: ——— motos praestat componere fluctus,
[… it’s better to calm the troubled waters,]

div.p: I have overshot myself, I have spoken foolishly, rashly, unadvisedly, absurdly, I have anatomized mine own folly. And now methinks upon a sudden I am awaked as it were out of a dream, I have had a raving fit, a fantastical fit, ranged up and down, in and out, I have insulted over most kind of men, abused some, offended others, wronged myself; and now being recovered, and perceiving mine error, cry with Ariost. lib. 39 Staf. 58.Orlando, Solvite me, pardon (o boni [good men!]) that which is past, and I will make you amends in that which is to come; I promise you a more sober discourse in my following Treatise.

If through weakness, folly, passion, Ut enim ex studiis gaudium sic studia ex hilaritate proveniunt [For even as joy proceeds from study, so study proceeds from laughter]. Plinius Maximo suo, ep. lib. 8.discontent, ignorance, I have said amiss, let it be forgotten and forgiven. I acknowledge that of Annal. 15.Tacitus to be true, Asperae facetiae ubi nimis ex vero traxere, acrem sui memoriam relinquunt, a bitter jest leaves a sting behind it; and as an honourable man observes, Sir Francis Bacon in his Essays, now Viscount St. Albans.They fear a Satirist’s wit, he their memories. I may justly suspect the worst; and though I hope I have wronged no man, yet in Medea’s words I will crave pardon,

lg.l: ——— Illud jam voce extrema peto,

l.hi: Ne si qua noster dubius effudit dolor,
Maneant in animo verba, sed melior tibi
Memoria nostri subeat, haec irae data

lg.l: Obliterentur ———
And in my last words this I do desire,
That what in passion I have said, or ire,
May be forgotten, and a better mind
Be had of us, hereafter as you find.

div.p:
I earnestly request every private man, as Scaliger did Cardan, not to take offence. I will conclude in his lines, Si me cognitum haberes, non solum donares nobis has facetias nostras, sed etiam indignum duceres, tam humanum animum, lene ingenium, vel minimam suspitionem deprecari oportere. If thou knewest my Quod Probus Persii βιογράφος virginali verecundia Persium fuisse dicit, ego, &c. [Because Probus, biographer of Persius, says that Persius was of a virginal modesty, I, etc.]modesty and simplicity, thou wouldst easily pardon and forgive what is here amiss, or by thee misconceived. If hereafter anatomizing this surly humour, my hand slip, as an unskilful prentice I lance too deep, and cut through skin and all
at unawares, make it smart, or cut awry, Quas aut incuria fudit, aut humana parum cavit natura [What negligence let slip, or human nature heeded too little]. Hor.pardon a rude hand, an unskilful knife, ’tis a most difficult thing to keep an even tone, a perpetual tenor, and not sometimes to lash out; difficile est Satyram non scribere [it’s hard not to write satire], there be so many objects to divert, inward perturbations to molest, and the very best may sometimes err; aliquando bonus dormitat Homerus [sometimes good Homer is sleepy], it is impossible not in so much to overshoot:

lg.l: ——— opere in longo fas est obrepere somnum.
[… in a long work, you’re allowed to let sleep creep up on you.]

div.p: But what needs all this? I hope there will no such cause of offence be given; if there be,

lg.l: Prol. quer. Plaut.Nemo aliquid recognoscat, nos mentimur omnia.
[Nobody should take anything personally: we lie about everything.]

div.p: I’ll deny all (my last refuge), recant all, renounce all I have said, if any man except, and with as much facility excuse, as he can accuse; but I presume of thy good favour, and gracious acceptance (gentle reader), out of an assured hope and confidence thereof, I will begin.
